paper.title: LEA: A 128-Bit Block Cipher for Fast Encryption on Common Processors

program.how: written for ounce-core from the algorithm description; no third-party code copied
program.target: static freestanding aarch64 Linux ELF, run with `ounce-core run-elf`

claims_checked: LEA with 128-, 192- and 256-bit keys: 30 of 30 ECB, 30 of 30 CBC and 30 of 30 CTR known-answer messages match (90 of 90; 10 per mode and key length, up to 400 bytes)

expected_values_source.what: the Crypto++ test-vector file lea.txt, whose entries cite "LEA reference test vectors, file lea_vs.c" (the designers' reference vector file). The eight key-schedule constants are the fractional hexadecimal digits of sqrt(766965), recomputed during development with integer arithmetic
expected_values_source.note: the vectors are relayed by Crypto++, not fetched from KISA; the paper PDF was not fetched. Data copied as numbers; no code was copied

negative_control: built with LEA_ROT_A=8 (rotation 8 instead of 9 in the first output word), 0 of 30 ECB, 0 of 30 CBC and 0 of 30 CTR vectors match, program exits 1
not_checked: security claims, speed figures (the paper's main claim is fast software encryption)
Tier-4 and native ARM64 execution (the native comparison is x86-64)
speed figures (emulator run time says nothing about the authors' hardware)
what_a_pass_means: this program, run on ounce-core, produces the 90 reference LEA ciphertexts for their inputs. It does not show the cipher is secure.
